subject: Fluctuation in Significance between Models with procD.pgls

messages.subject: Fluctuation in Significance between Models with procD.pgls
parts:
Hello,

I am trying to compare a few different possible models for explaining my data with procD.pgls (mainly trying to see if incorporating size leads to a significantly better model), and along the way discovered that some of my variables flip flop between being significant and non-significant (sometimes by quite a bit) depending on the model. For reference, I am working with a dataset of 3-D landmarks of skulls, with a paired ecological dataset of two grouping variables, Habitat Use and Diet. I abbreviate the r output below for a few examples, with P-values bolded. Any thoughts on whether this should be expected and possible recommendations for interpreting and choosing the most meaningful model?

When I incorporate a model that just includes diet as an independent variable it is very insignificant:

> summary(procD.pgls(coords ~ Diet, phy=phy, data=allo_notroph, SS.type="III"))
 
           Df      SS        MS     Rsq      F        Z Pr(>F)
Diet        9 0.01282 0.0014249 0.01845 0.2882 -0.96077  0.839
Residuals 138 0.68231 0.0049443 0.98155                      
Total     147 0.69513                           

When also including habitat use, and the interaction between habitat use and diet - diet now becomes significant:

> summary(procD.pgls(coords ~ Diet*Habitat_Use, phy=phy, data=allo_notroph, SS.type="III"))

                  Df      SS         MS      Rsq      F      Z Pr(>F)  
Diet               9 0.01169 0.00129856 0.016813 1.5110 1.8706  0.048 *
Habitat_Use        6 0.00903 0.00150473 0.012988 1.7510 2.3187  0.019 *
Diet:Habitat_Use  17 0.02561 0.00150644 0.036841 1.7529 3.4639  0.001 **
Residuals        115 0.09883 0.00085938 0.142172                        
Total            147 0.69513                                            

With habitat use, diet, and size, but without their interactions, just habitat use and size are significant:

> summary(procD.pgls(coords ~ Diet+Habitat_Use+log(cs), phy=phy, data=allo_notroph, SS.type="III"))

             Df      SS        MS      Rsq       F      Z Pr(>F)  
Diet          9 0.00907 0.0010077 0.013046  1.1261 0.5915  0.286  
Habitat_Use   6 0.12488 0.0208134 0.179650 23.2604 9.9262  0.001 **
log(cs)       1 0.00722 0.0072188 0.010385  8.0675 5.5106  0.001 **
Residuals   131 0.11722 0.0008948 0.168629                        
Total       147 0.69513                                            

And in the most complicated model, when including all variables and also including their interactions, everything becomes insignificant other than size:

> summary(procD.pgls(coords ~ Diet*Habitat_Use*log(cs), phy=phy, data=allo_notroph, SS.type="III"))

                          Df      SS         MS      Rsq      F       Z Pr(>F)  
Diet                       9 0.00963 0.00106994 0.013853 1.3791 1.31152  0.104  
Habitat_Use                6 0.00577 0.00096187 0.008302 1.2398 0.86122  0.188  
log(cs)                    1 0.00208 0.00207874 0.002990 2.6794 1.96679  0.034 *
Diet:Habitat_Use          17 0.01488 0.00087520 0.021404 1.1281 0.74044  0.222  
Diet:log(cs)               6 0.00521 0.00086898 0.007501 1.1201 0.49410  0.298  
Habitat_Use:log(cs)        5 0.00402 0.00080469 0.005788 1.0372 0.21459  0.413  
Diet:Habitat_Use:log(cs)   8 0.00729 0.00091134 0.010488 1.1747 0.75706  0.215  
Residuals                 95 0.07370 0.00077581 0.106026                        
Total                    147 0.69513                                            

Visually when inspecting my data in a PCA, habitat use does look like the strongest influence, with a visible, but more minor effect of size (allometry) in some groups. Diet doesn't seem to be much of an influence (at least visually), but does appear to covary with diet in some groups. So much of the above statistical results make intuitive sense to me, however, I am still struggling to understand why a variable (like diet) might come out as very insignificant when modeled by itself, but when taking habitat use into account, becomes significant. And then why going from a model like coords ~ Diet+Habitat_Use+log(cs) results in pretty different significance values for variables compared to the more complex coords ~ Diet*Habitat_Use*log(cs).

Any thoughts would be much appreciated.

Thanks,
Greg

parts:
Greg,

 

It is impossible to provide a stock answer to whether or not what you observe with Diet “is expected” for all situations. What I can say is that one’s intuition as to whether the ‘strength’ of effect explained by a factor when included in various models is not as straight forward as the post implies. To truly understand what is expected, one must consider both the full (hypothesis) model, and its reduced model(s); the latter of which also changes based on the sums-of-squares types one chooses to use.

 

Consider your example. You have models like:

 

Shape ~ diet

Shape ~ diet + many things

Shape ~ diet + many (some other) things

 

These define your full(hypothesis) models, and are fine.  Now, the other critical thing to consider is that you are using marginal (type III) SS.  This defines the reduced models for each term in your model.  Recall that type III SS are ‘exclusion-based’; meaning that the importance of a variable in terms of its SS is calculated by subtraction: what component of SS changes when that variable is removed from the model, given that the rest of the explanatory variables remain in the model. 

 

So to your example you have (shape = Y for simplicity below):

 

FULL                                      REDUCED

Y ~ diet                                 Y ~ 1

Y ~ diet + many                 Y ~ many

Y ~ diet + many.2             Y ~ many.2

 

Thus, the effect of diet is evaluated relative to the overall mean model, or a model including many, or including many.2.  That could change a great deal, depending upon what is in ‘many’.  This is what you observed.

 

Was this surprising? Not really. It is only surprising if one has the expectation that the effect of a term in a model is unchanged across models (i.e,. ignores the reduced model against which it is compared). 

 

I suggest a careful read of statistical theory on sums-of-squares, what they do and don’t tell us, how they are calculated, and of course the literature on model comparison. This might help one’s intuition match what the math is revealing.


Best,

 

Dean
